title: JVM memory & runtime
scopeHtml: Scope: runtime memory areas, object layout, class loading, JIT, CDS/AOT, native image (brief), escape analysis and JVM behaviour in containers. GC algorithms and leak diagnosis belong to the next two chunks.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the memory areas of a running HotSpot JVM. Which of them are inside -Xmx and which are not?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who think "JVM memory = heap" cannot explain why a container is OOM-killed while the heap looks healthy.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I split it into heap, which -Xmx caps, and everything else, which it does not cap. Heap holds objects and arrays. Outside it: Metaspace for class metadata, the code cache for JIT-compiled code, one stack per thread, direct and mapped buffers, and GC and JVM internal structures. The process RSS is the sum of all of that, so the container limit has to cover the whole sum, not just -Xmx.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
OS process memory (RSS)
+-- Java heap (-Xms/-Xmx)           objects, arrays, (strings, boxed values)
+-- Metaspace (native, no cap)      class metadata: methods, constant pools, vtables
|     +-- Compressed class space    Klass structures (default 1 GB reserved)
+-- Code cache (240 MB tiered)      interpreter stubs + C1/C2 machine code
+-- Thread stacks (1 MB default     one per platform thread, committed lazily
|   on Linux x64)
+-- Direct / mapped buffers         ByteBuffer.allocateDirect, Netty, mmap files
+-- GC structures                   G1 remembered sets, card tables, mark bitmaps
+-- Other native                    JIT compiler arenas, symbol tables, JNI, malloc arenas, libs

Java 8 removed PermGen (class metadata moved from heap to native Metaspace). Metaspace has no limit by default (MaxMetaspaceSize is unlimited), so a class leak grows until the OS or container stops you. Heap sizing in containers is covered in the container questions below. A rough rule: non-heap is commonly 10-25% on top of heap for a typical Spring service, but measure with NMT (-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary) rather than trusting rules.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Seeing the split on a live process:

java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary -Xmx1g -jar app.jar &
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary   # committed per area: Java Heap, Class, Thread, Code, GC, Internal...

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "stack stores primitives, heap stores objects"; stack holds frames (locals, operand stack), and a local reference points to a heap object.
  • Believing -Xmx limits process memory.
  • Saying Metaspace is "part of heap" or "PermGen renamed".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What replaced PermGen and why? → Metaspace in Java 8; PermGen had a fixed size that required tuning and caused OOM on redeploys; Metaspace grows in native memory.
  2. Which area does -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize limit? → Only NIO direct buffers allocated through ByteBuffer.allocateDirect, not all native memory.
  3. How would you account for 3 GB RSS with a 1 GB heap? → NMT summary, then compare against pmap//proc/<pid>/smaps to catch what NMT cannot see (glibc malloc arenas, native libraries).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer lists heap, stack, Metaspace. The senior answer ties each area to a failure mode and a measurement tool, and states that the container limit must budget the sum.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: The classic Kubernetes incident: pod limit 2 GiB, -Xmx2g, pod OOMKilled with a clean heap. See the dedicated scenario below.

questions.promptHtml: What exactly lives on the stack and what lives on the heap in Java? What causes StackOverflowError, and can you size the stack?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks the mental model of references vs objects, and whether you know thread-count x stack-size is a real memory cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each thread has its own stack of frames; a frame holds local variables, the operand stack and return info. Primitives and references live in frames; every object and array lives on the heap (escape analysis can sometimes eliminate the allocation, but that is an optimisation, not a semantic). StackOverflowError means the thread's stack ran out, normally from unbounded or very deep recursion. Size it with -Xss or -XX:ThreadStackSize; default is 1 MB on Linux x64.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• A call pushes a frame; return pops it. Frame size is fixed at compile time per method (max locals + max stack depth in the class file), so depth x frame size must fit the stack.
  • 1 MB stack typically gives roughly 10-20k simple frames; JIT-compiled frames are often smaller than interpreted ones, so the same code can overflow at different depths before and after warmup. Never hardcode a depth assumption.
  • Stack memory is reserved virtual address space and committed as touched, so 500 idle threads do not cost 500 MB of RSS up front, but each thread's touched pages stay committed.
  • Heap is shared by all threads, so objects reachable from several threads need synchronisation; stack data is thread-confined by construction.
  • -Xss applies to new Java threads; the main thread's stack on Linux is set by the launcher (and ulimit -s for the primordial thread), so tuning -Xss may not affect main.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: unbounded recursion on user-controlled depth
static int depth(Node n) { return n == null ? 0 : 1 + depth(n.next); }   // 200k-long list => StackOverflowError

// Fix: iterate
static int depthIter(Node n) { int d = 0; while (n != null) { d++; n = n.next; } return d; }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Raising -Xss globally to "fix" a recursion bug: multiplies by every thread (1000 threads x 2 MB = 2 GB reserved).
  • Catching StackOverflowError and continuing; locks and invariants may be half-updated.
  • Assuming objects are "always on heap" and then being confused by escape analysis results.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is StackOverflowError an Exception? → No, an Error (VirtualMachineError); app code should not normally catch it.
  2. Where do static fields and interned strings live? → Static fields live with the Class mirror object on the heap; interned strings are in the heap string table since Java 7.
  3. How do virtual threads change stack memory? → Their stacks are heap-allocated stack chunks that grow and shrink; covered in the virtual-threads chunk.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE defines stack and heap. Senior adds frame sizing, interpreted vs compiled depth differences, lazy commit, and the per-thread multiplier when someone suggests bumping -Xss.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A recursive JSON/graph walker passed unit tests, then overflowed in production on a 50k-deep user-supplied structure; the fix was an iterative traversal plus a depth limit at the input boundary.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how a class gets loaded in the JVM: the phases, the loader hierarchy and parent delegation. Why does delegation exist?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Foundation for ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError, classloader leaks, app servers and plugin systems.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Loading reads the bytes and creates the Class; linking verifies, prepares (static defaults) and resolves; initialization runs static initializers, lazily, on first active use. Loaders delegate to their parent first, so core classes like java.lang.String always come from the bootstrap loader and cannot be spoofed by application code.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Loading -> Linking[ Verification -> Preparation -> Resolution ] -> Initialization
(bytes -> Class)   (bytecode safe)  (statics=0/null)  (symbolic->direct, may be lazy)  (<clinit> runs)
  • Java 9+ hierarchy: bootstrap (native, java.base etc.) -> platform loader -> application (system) loader -> custom loaders. Java 8 had bootstrap -> extension -> application.
  • Delegation: loadClass(name) checks if already loaded by this loader, asks the parent, and only then calls findClass. Guarantees core types are unique and secure.
  • A class's identity is (name, defining loader). The same bytes loaded by two loaders are two distinct, incompatible types (ClassCastException "X cannot be cast to X"). Plugin/app-server isolation relies on this; Tomcat's webapp loader deliberately reverses delegation for webapp classes.
  • Initialization is triggered by new, static method call, non-constant static field access, reflection, subclass init. It is thread-safe: the JVM holds an init lock per class, which is why a static initializer cycle between two classes on two threads can deadlock.
  • NoClassDefFoundError: class was present at compile time but failed to load or its static init failed earlier (second access gives NoClassDefFoundError after an ExceptionInInitializerError). ClassNotFoundException: explicit load by name (Class.forName) failed.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Holder {
    static final Map<String,String> M = load();   // if load() throws, first use => ExceptionInInitializerError,
    static Map<String,String> load() { throw new IllegalStateException("config missing"); }  // later uses => NoClassDefFoundError
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking classes load at startup; most load lazily on first resolution.
  • Confusing Class.forName (initializes) with ClassLoader.loadClass (does not initialize).
  • Ignoring that two copies of a library in different loaders produce type mismatches.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError? → Checked failure to find by name vs linkage error for a class that was there at compile time or whose init failed.
  2. How do you find which jar a class came from? → Foo.class.getProtectionDomain().getCodeSource() or -verbose:class / -Xlog:class+load.
  3. Why can a class loader leak memory? → A loaded class holds its loader, the loader holds all its classes; any live reference (thread, ThreadLocal, static in parent loader) pins the whole graph and Metaspace. Diagnosis is in the memory-leak chunk.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE recites the three loaders. Senior explains identity = (name, loader), lazy init and its locking, and why the same class can fail casts across loaders.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fat-jar app and a shaded agent both bundled different versions of a library; NoSuchMethodError appeared only on one code path, found through -Xlog:class+load showing the unexpected jar.

questions.promptHtml: How many bytes does new Object() take on a 64-bit JVM? What is in an object header, and how much does an Integer, an int[1], and an object with two int fields cost?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Memory estimation is a senior skill; the follow-up is always "so why is a List<Integer> expensive?".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: On HotSpot 64-bit with default compressed class pointers, the header is 12 bytes (8-byte mark word plus 4-byte class pointer), and objects are aligned to 8 bytes, so new Object() is 16 bytes. Integer is 12 + 4 = 16 bytes, an int[1] is 12 + 4 length + 4 data = 20, rounded to 24, and a two-int object is 12 + 8 = 20, rounded to 24. Without compressed class pointers the header is 16 bytes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Object (compressed class pointers):  [mark word 8][klass 4] [fields...] [pad to 8]
Array:                               [mark word 8][klass 4][length 4][elements...][pad to 8]
  • Mark word holds identity hash, GC age, lock state. Klass pointer points to class metadata in Metaspace.
  • Field layout is chosen by the JVM (larger fields first, gaps filled), not source order.
  • References are 4 bytes with compressed oops (heap < ~32 GB), otherwise 8.
  • Take Integer: 16 bytes vs 4 for a raw int, plus the 4-byte reference pointing to it: a List<Integer> element costs ~20 bytes vs 4 for int[], so about 5x, plus pointer-chasing cache misses.
  • JEP 450 (Java 24) experimental: compact object headers shrink the header to 8 bytes (-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders). I believe it became a product feature in a later release (JEP 519); verify for the JDK you run.
  • Check with JOL (org.openjdk.jol:jol-core) instead of guessing.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import org.openjdk.jol.info.ClassLayout;
System.out.println(ClassLayout.parseClass(Integer.class).toPrintable());
System.out.println(ClassLayout.parseInstance(new int[1]).toPrintable());

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using Runtime.totalMemory()-freeMemory() deltas to measure object size; TLABs and GC make it noisy.
  • Forgetting alignment padding when summing field sizes.
  • Quoting "16 byte header" as universal; it depends on compression flags and JDK version.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is Long 24 bytes with compressed headers? → 12 header, 4 padding so the 8-byte long is 8-aligned at offset 16, then 8 = 24.
  2. What does Integer caching do to this? → Integer.valueOf reuses instances for -128..127, so small values don't allocate; large ones do.
  3. How does object size affect GC? → Allocation rate and live-set bytes drive GC cost; shrinking per-object overhead cuts both. Detail is in the GC chunks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "an object has a header". Senior computes sizes, knows the compression flags and the effect on collection-heavy workloads.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cache of 20M Map<Long, Long> entries needed several GB because of node and boxing overhead; see the footprint scenario below.

questions.promptHtml: What are compressed oops? Why do teams say "don't go above 32 GB heap", and what actually happens at that boundary?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand a real sizing cliff and can reason about trade-offs instead of "bigger heap is better".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With compressed oops the JVM stores object references as 32-bit values, shifted left by 3 because objects are 8-byte aligned, so 32 bits address 2^35 bytes, about 32 GB. Cross that and references become 64-bit, which makes every reference field and array of references twice as large. A 33 GB heap can hold less live data than a 31 GB heap.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Decode: address = heap_base + (ref << 3). If the heap sits in the first 4 GB, no shift or base needed ("32-bit mode"); up to about 32 GB the "zero-based" mode needs only a shift; higher placement needs base add ("non-zero based"). Each mode is slightly slower than the one before, so slightly under the limit is best.
  • Alignment can be raised: -XX:ObjectAlignmentInBytes=16 extends the compressed range to ~64 GB but wastes padding on small objects. Rarely worth it; measure.
  • The JVM auto-disables compressed oops when -Xmx exceeds the range; -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal | grep UseCompressedOops or the startup log shows what happened. Quote from Shipilev's quark: a dataset that fit in a 31 GB heap needed about 36 GB once references doubled, roughly 40% more.
  • Practical ceiling is typically a few GB under 32, depending on platform and mode, so teams often pick 31 GB or lower. Verify with -Xlog:gc+init or jcmd <pid> VM.flags on your JVM.
  • Class pointers (UseCompressedClassPointers) are a separate setting (decoupled from oops in modern JDKs; verify the version in your fleet).
  • ZGC historically did not support compressed oops (it uses coloured 64-bit pointers); verify for current JDK versions, as this changes the heap-sizing advice there.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
java -Xmx31g -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E "UseCompressedOops|ObjectAlignmentInBytes"
java -Xmx33g -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E "UseCompressedOops"   # false

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Scaling a service from 24 GB to 40 GB heap and seeing worse GC and no capacity gain.
  • Setting -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 on a large node, silently landing above the cliff.
  • Forgetting that object-heavy heaps (pointer-rich) are hit harder than primitive-array-heavy ones.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you verify your heap uses compressed oops? → jcmd <pid> VM.flags, PrintFlagsFinal, or -Xlog:gc+heap+coops.
  2. What do you do if the working set truly needs 60 GB? → Go well past the cliff (e.g., 48+ GB), or shard, or go off-heap/primitive structures; test both.
  3. Does it matter for ZGC/Shenandoah? → Different pointer handling; check the current docs for your JDK before assuming.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE repeats "keep heap under 32 GB". Senior explains shift-by-3, alignment, the three modes, the real capacity loss past the cliff and how to confirm it on a live JVM.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team resized pods from 28 GB to 36 GB heap hoping to cut GC frequency; throughput fell because references doubled and cache locality worsened.

questions.contextHtml: A Spring Boot order service runs on Kubernetes (Java 17, G1) with resources.limits.memory: 2Gi and JAVA_OPTS=-Xms2g -Xmx2g. Since Monday's release (new Netty-based HTTP client and a larger Caffeine cache) pods restart every 6-10 hours. kubectl describe pod shows Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137. The application log has no OutOfMemoryError. Grafana's jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap"} peaks at 1.4 GB. Traffic is 400 RPS, steady. A colleague says "Java is leaking, let's add -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError".
questions.promptHtml: Explain what is happening and how you would fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the memory limit to 4Gi" or "take a heap dump and look for leaks". Neither explains why heap is only 1.4 GB, and a heap dump will not exist because the JVM never threw an OOM; the kernel killed it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it OOMKilled (kernel, cgroup) or a Java OOME? Exit 137 plus no Java log says kernel. What is container_memory_working_set_bytes doing over time: flat at the limit or sawtoothing up? Are thread count and direct buffer metrics available (jvm_threads_live, jvm_buffer_memory_used_bytes)? Is there anything native in the new release?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll the heap to -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60 (about 1.2 GiB of 2 GiB), or temporarily raise the limit to 3Gi to stop restarts while I diagnose.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) -Xmx equals the limit, so any non-heap use pushes RSS past the cgroup limit; (b) Netty direct buffers growing outside heap; (c) Metaspace / thread stacks grew with the new release; (d) glibc malloc arena fragmentation; (e) a true native leak (least likely, check last).
  4. How I'd verify each: Restart with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, take jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline and summary.diff a few hours later; jcmd <pid> VM.info; compare RSS to NMT total; Micrometer jvm_buffer_memory_used_bytes{id="direct"}; jstack-count threads.
  5. Root cause: Budget math: heap 2048 MB (fully committed with -Xms=-Xmx) + Metaspace ~150 + code cache ~60 + 200 threads x 1 MB = 200 + Netty direct ~300 + G1 remembered sets/card tables/bitmaps ~150-250 + malloc/other ~100 = about 3.0-3.1 GB against a 2 GiB limit. The pod hits the cgroup limit; the kernel kills it before the heap fills. The heap graph looked fine because the heap was never the problem.
  6. Fix: Short-term: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60 and limit 2.5Gi. Long-term: cap -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize (e.g. 256m), fix Netty's allocator settings, set memory request = limit, and size from NMT numbers.
env:
  - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
    value: "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60 -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=256m -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary"
resources: { requests: { memory: 2560Mi }, limits: { memory: 2560Mi } }
  1. Prevention: Alert on working-set / limit > 85%; dashboard heap + non-heap + buffers + threads stacked; a startup log line of effective MaxHeap; a load test in staging at production limits.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just raise the limit (hides the budget bug and costs money for 60 pods), and not set heap to 50% blindly: for small pods that wastes memory; for big ones 75% may be fine. Recommend measuring.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• NMT shows total committed 2.2 GB but RSS is 2.9 GB, why? → NMT does not track everything (native libraries, glibc arena fragmentation); try MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 and compare pmap.
  • Would -Xmx below the limit also stop the kill if direct buffers leak? → No, a direct-memory leak still grows RSS; cap MaxDirectMemorySize so it fails as a Java OOM with a stack trace instead of a silent kill.
  • Is -Xms=-Xmx a mistake? → Not inherently (avoids resize), but it commits all heap up front, which removes slack in a tight budget.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite from several teams: a pod fleet had "random" restarts for weeks; each team added heap and limit. The first NMT diff showed Thread and Internal growth from an unbounded executor; the heap graph never moved.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: asks for more memory or a heap dump; cannot say who kills the process.
  • Hire: identifies cgroup OOM vs Java OOM, non-heap budget, and sets a percentage-based heap.
  • Strong hire: does the arithmetic, uses NMT diff, caps direct memory, explains exit code 137, and sets request = limit with alerts.

questions.promptHtml: Explain HotSpot's tiered compilation. What are the tiers, what triggers promotion, and why does a Java service get faster after minutes of running?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who know "JIT exists" from those who can explain warmup, profile-guided optimisation and latency after deploys.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Code starts in the interpreter, which also collects counters. Hot methods go to C1 (quick, lightly optimised), at level 3 with full profiling, and the hottest go to C2 (slow to compile, heavily optimised using that profile) at level 4. Performance rises as C2 finishes compiling the real hot paths, which is why a cold JVM is slow for the first seconds to minutes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Level 0 interpreter (counts invocations + loop back-edges)
Level 1 C1, no profiling      (trivial methods, final stop)
Level 2 C1, limited profiling (used when C2 queue is long)
Level 3 C1, full profiling    (default path)  ---> hot enough --->  Level 4 C2 (optimised, profile-guided)
  • Triggers are invocation and back-edge counters against per-tier thresholds, scaled by compile-queue load. One source I read lists Tier4InvocationThreshold=5000, Tier4CompileThreshold=15000 and Tier4BackEdgeThreshold=40000 (older JDK output; verify on your version with -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal). Level 3 triggers much earlier (around 200 invocations, verify).
  • Hot loops in a method called once are handled by OSR (on-stack replacement): a compiled version is entered mid-loop.
  • C2 uses profile data (branch frequencies, receiver types) to inline aggressively, devirtualise, and speculate, with deoptimisation as the safety net (see the deopt question).
  • Compilation runs in background compiler threads (count scales with CPUs). A CPU-throttled container slows compilation and so lengthens warmup.
  • Tiered is on by default since Java 8; -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 gives C1 only: faster startup, lower peak, useful for short-lived CLI/serverless jobs. -Xint disables JIT (diagnostic only). Seeing it: -XX:+PrintCompilation, or jcmd <pid> Compiler.queue.
  • Many JIT facts shifted over versions (JVMCI, Graal as compiler removed from JDK in 17): check the release docs.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
java -XX:+PrintCompilation -jar app.jar | head -50
# columns: timestamp, id, flags (% = OSR, ! = has exception handler), tier level, method, size
java -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+LogCompilation -XX:LogFile=jit.log -jar app.jar

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Benchmarking a cold run with System.nanoTime and concluding Java is slow.
  • Calling C1 "the client compiler" and C2 "the server compiler" as though you choose between them; with tiered both run.
  • Forgetting that profile pollution (megamorphic call sites) limits what C2 can do.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is OSR? → Switching a long-running loop from interpreted to compiled code mid-execution.
  2. How do you mitigate warmup in autoscaling? → Readiness gating with warmup traffic, gradual ramp-up, CDS/AOT cache for class loading, or native image trade-offs; see the warmup scenario.
  3. Why can C2 be faster than ahead-of-time compiled code? → It has runtime profile data and can speculate with deopt as a fallback.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "hot code gets compiled". Senior names tiers, counters, OSR, background compile threads and links CPU throttling to warmup latency.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After autoscaling, new pods served p99 3x slower for ~90 s; compile queue and CPU throttling were the cause, not GC.

questions.promptHtml: What is stored in Metaspace, how does it grow and shrink, and when can a class actually be unloaded?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Metaspace growth is a top "heap fine, process dying" cause; interviewers want to see you connect it to loaders, not just flags.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Metaspace holds class metadata: method bytecode, constant pools, field and method descriptors, vtables. It lives in native memory and is unlimited by default, so unbounded class generation grows it until the OS stops you. A class is unloaded only when its defining class loader becomes unreachable and a GC cycle notices, so classes from the bootstrap, platform or app loaders effectively never unload.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Allocation is per class loader (arenas); memory returns to the OS only when the loader dies and its chunks are freed. Thus fragmentation and a few long-lived loaders can keep Metaspace committed long after peak.
  • -XX:MetaspaceSize is a high-water mark that triggers a GC to try unloading (not a floor or cap); -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize is the cap (unlimited by default). Setting a cap converts a slow leak into a clear OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace, which is usually what you want in a container. Compressed class space (-XX:CompressedClassSpaceSize, default 1 GB reserved) holds the Klass structures and can also overflow ("Compressed class space").
  • Unloading happens during GC. G1 can unload classes in concurrent cycles; ZGC and Shenandoah unload concurrently. Full details of collectors are in the GC chunks.
  • Who generates classes at runtime: CGLIB/ByteBuddy proxies (Spring AOP, Hibernate), Groovy/Nashorn scripts, JSP compilation, Proxy.newProxyInstance, lambdas (hidden classes, unloadable with their lookup), reflection inflation accessors (older JDKs).
  • Monitoring: jstat -gc <pid> columns MC/MU, jcmd <pid> VM.metaspace, jcmd <pid> VM.classloader_stats, Micrometer jvm_classes_loaded_classes and jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="nonheap",id="Metaspace"}, -Xlog:class+unload.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
java -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m -Xlog:class+unload=info -jar app.jar
jcmd <pid> VM.classloader_stats          # classes per loader, spot a loader with 30k classes

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating -XX:MetaspaceSize as the maximum.
  • Leaving no cap, then wondering why the OOM-killer fires instead of a Java error.
  • Assuming a GC cycle always frees Metaspace; reachable loaders pin it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does Metaspace sometimes not shrink after unloading? → Chunk-based allocation and fragmentation; freed to the OS lazily.
  2. Why do hot-redeploys leak Metaspace? → A thread, ThreadLocal or static in a parent loader holds the old webapp loader; leak diagnosis is in the memory-leak chunk.
  3. How is PermGen different? → Fixed size, inside the heap-ish managed region, tied to full GC; Metaspace is native and elastic.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "Metaspace replaced PermGen and stores class info". Senior explains the loader-lifetime rule, per-loader arenas, the caps and the generators of classes in typical Spring stacks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Setting MaxMetaspaceSize turned silent RSS growth into a crisp Metaspace OOM with a stack trace pointing at a dynamic proxy factory.

questions.promptHtml: What is direct (off-heap) memory in Java? Why do Netty and Kafka clients use it, how is it freed, and how is it limited?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Direct memory is invisible to heap graphs, and mismanaging it causes both OOMs and kills.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ByteBuffer.allocateDirect allocates native memory outside the heap, avoiding a copy between a heap array and the kernel when doing I/O and keeping big buffers out of the GC's way. The JVM frees it only when the small heap-side DirectByteBuffer object is collected and its cleaner runs, so a quiet heap can delay freeing of lots of native memory. The total is capped by -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, which when unset defaults to roughly the max heap size (verify your version).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• I/O with a heap buffer: the JDK copies to a temporary direct buffer before the syscall; direct buffers skip that copy.
  • Each allocation reserves against the limit (Bits.reserveMemory). If the limit is hit, the JVM triggers System.gc() hoping to free unreferenced buffers, sleeps briefly and retries, then throws OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory. Hence -XX:+DisableExplicitGC combined with heavy direct buffer use is dangerous (it removes that safety valve).
  • Allocation is slower than heap allocation and zeroes memory; pool and reuse buffers. Netty has its own pooled allocator (PooledByteBufAllocator) with reference counting; a missing release() leaks native memory with no heap signature. Netty also tracks usage against -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize; check its docs for the exact behaviour per version.
  • Memory-mapped files (FileChannel.map) are another off-heap area, counted in the page cache and RSS but not in direct-memory limits.
  • Java 21+ Foreign Function & Memory API (Arena, MemorySegment) is the modern, deterministically-closed alternative; its finalized status depends on release (Java 22 finalized per JEP 454; verify).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(1 << 20);   // 1 MiB native; cleaned only after buf is GC'd
// FFM API alternative with deterministic lifetime (Java 22+):
try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) {
    MemorySegment seg = arena.allocate(1 << 20);       // freed at try-exit
}
-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=512m
# Metrics: jvm_buffer_memory_used_bytes{id="direct"}; also BufferPoolMXBean "direct"

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Allocating a fresh direct buffer per request instead of pooling.
  • Forgetting Netty ReferenceCountUtil.release() on unhandled messages.
  • Believing a heap dump will show the problem; the heap holds only tiny buffer wrappers.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you see direct memory use? → BufferPoolMXBean, NMT, Micrometer buffer metrics, Netty's PlatformDependent.usedDirectMemory().
  2. Why does it OOM when the heap is nearly empty? → The cap is separate; frees depend on GC of the wrappers, and an idle young gen may not collect them.
  3. Is direct memory counted by the cgroup? → Yes, it is RSS; the container limit must budget for it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows "off-heap, faster I/O". Senior knows the cleaner mechanism, the System.gc() retry loop, the explicit-GC trap and budgets the cap inside the container.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After switching a client library to a Netty transport, pods died of Direct buffer memory under bursts; pooling plus a 256 MB cap fixed it.

questions.contextHtml: A Java 17 payment-lookup service (G1, 4 vCPU request, limit 4 vCPU, 4 GiB) averages p99 = 60 ms. HPA scales from 6 to 24 pods at a peak. Each new pod becomes Ready 25 s after start (readiness probe hits /health), receives its fair share of traffic immediately, and for the first ~2 minutes shows p99 = 900 ms and 10% timeouts (client timeout 500 ms). Cluster-wide p99 triples during every scale-up. GC logs of new pods look normal (young pauses 10-20 ms). CPU on new pods is pegged at 100% of limit for the first minute, then falls to 55%. A teammate wants to "tune G1".
questions.promptHtml: Why do new pods perform badly, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Tune GC" or "add more pods earlier". It ignores that the pods are CPU-bound by compilation and class loading, and that readiness only checks liveness, not warmness.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the pegged CPU show in compiler threads? How many classes are loaded at Ready time? Do requests touch lazily initialised things (Hibernate metadata, connection pools, caches)? Is the CPU limit equal to request (throttling)? What is the autoscale trigger lag?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Lower the HPA scale-up trigger so pods start earlier; add a startup/readiness delay plus a gradual traffic ramp (service mesh slow start, e.g. Envoy slow-start, or Nginx slow_start).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) JIT warmup: interpreter and C1 code is 10-50x slower than C2 on hot paths, and compile threads compete with request threads for 4 vCPU; (b) lazy class loading and Spring/Hibernate initialisation on first requests; (c) CFS throttling on the CPU limit; (d) cold caches (app caches, DNS, connection establishment); (e) GC (red herring: logs look fine).
  4. How I'd verify each: -XX:+PrintCompilation or JFR jdk.Compilation events over the first minute; jcmd <pid> Compiler.queue for backlog; -Xlog:class+load count vs time; container metric container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total; async-profiler wall-clock on a fresh pod (expect CompileBroker, ClassLoader.loadClass, <clinit>); compare p99 of the same request at minute 1 vs minute 10.
  5. Root cause: Cold pods run mostly interpreted/C1 code while background C2 compiles queue behind each other on 4 vCPUs; first-touch class loading and initialisation also run on request threads. Readiness says "can answer", not "can answer at SLO".
  6. Fix: Short-term: warm-up routine before Ready (replay N synthetic requests covering hot paths, async-gated readiness); traffic slow-start over 60-120 s. Medium-term: AppCDS or the JDK 24+ AOT cache to cut class load/link time (JEP 483); eager-initialise lazy beans; give the pod a startup CPU boost (e.g. Kubernetes in-place resize or higher requests for startup) to speed compilation. Long-term: consider GraalVM native image only if startup is the main pain and peak throughput loss is acceptable.
readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }, initialDelaySeconds: 20, periodSeconds: 5 }
# /ready returns 200 only after the warmup runner has executed ~5k representative requests
  1. Prevention: A p99-by-pod-age dashboard; load test that includes cold-start; a deploy gate on warm p99.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not set -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 for a long-running service (caps peak throughput); not reduce -XX:CompileThreshold-style flags blindly (premature profiles can lead to deopt churn); not oversize the fleet permanently to hide warmup.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Warmup requests hit production dependencies; is that OK? → Use read-only or mocked/shadow dependencies; ensure warmup uses representative shapes, because profile pollution from unrepresentative traffic can mislead C2.
  • Would CRaC help? → Checkpoint/restore can start warm; vendor-dependent (e.g. Azul builds, Spring Boot CRaC support); verify availability and operational maturity.
  • Why 100% CPU at start? → Compiler threads, class loading/verification, bean creation and request handling compete; limits cap total.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team added warmup traffic but used one endpoint; C2 compiled that path perfectly, then the real mix hit megamorphic sites and triggered deopts. Replaying a sampled traffic mix fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: GC tuning only, no JIT or class loading awareness.
  • Hire: identifies warmup and throttling, proposes readiness warmup and slow-start.
  • Strong hire: verifies with JFR/profiling, adds CDS/AOT cache, discusses profile pollution and trade-offs of native image or CRaC.

questions.promptHtml: What is escape analysis in the JVM, and what does it enable? Does Java allocate objects on the stack?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The "Java puts non-escaping objects on the stack" claim is a common myth; the signal is knowing scalar replacement and its limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: C2 analyses whether an object can be seen outside the method (or thread) that created it. If it cannot escape, C2 can eliminate the allocation by scalar replacement, splitting the object into its fields held in registers, and can remove locks on it (lock elision). HotSpot does not do true stack allocation of objects; it removes the object entirely, and only when it can prove non-escape after inlining.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Categories: NoEscape (never leaves the method after inlining), ArgEscape (passed to a callee but not stored globally), GlobalEscape (stored in a field or returned). Scalar replacement applies to NoEscape.
  • Depends on inlining: if a callee is too big, megamorphic or not inlined, the object escapes into it and the optimisation is lost. That is why small, monomorphic helpers matter.
  • Done by C2 only; interpreter and C1 allocate normally, so benefits appear after warmup.
  • Controlled by -XX:+DoEscapeAnalysis (on by default). Compare with -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis in JMH with -prof gc and check gc.alloc.rate.norm.
  • Typical wins: short-lived value objects, Optional, iterators in simple loops, boxed values in tight code, StringBuilder in simple concatenation. Limits include large arrays (size cap, EliminateAllocationArraySizeLimit default 64 elements; verify), loops with phi merges and objects stored into arrays.
  • Not a design strategy: do not write ugly code assuming EA will save it; profile allocations (JFR allocation profiling, async-profiler alloc).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
record Point(double x, double y) {}
static double dist(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    Point a = new Point(x1, y1), b = new Point(x2, y2);   // after inlining neither escapes => no allocation
    return Math.hypot(a.x() - b.x(), a.y() - b.y());
}
// JMH: run with -prof gc and compare gc.alloc.rate.norm with/without -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming "objects go on the stack".
  • Micro-benchmarking without JMH and attributing results to EA.
  • Storing the object in a field "just for debugging" and silently defeating EA.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is lock elision? → If the lock object does not escape, synchronisation on it is dropped.
  2. Why does inlining matter? → EA works on the compilation unit after inlining; a non-inlined call makes the argument escape.
  3. How do you confirm EA fired? → JMH -prof gc allocation rate, or JFR allocation events, not guesses; diagnostic flags like -XX:+PrintEliminateAllocations need a debug build, verify.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "EA lets objects live on stack". Senior says scalar replacement, C2-only, inlining dependent, and how to prove it with JMH.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Allocation profile flame graphs showed an Optional wrapper in the hot path surviving because a lambda call site was megamorphic; replacing it with a plain null check cut allocation rate 30%.

questions.contextHtml: An ad-tech service keeps an in-memory lookup Map<Long, Long> (user id -> segment bitmask) refreshed daily. It holds 50 million entries. The service runs on Java 17 with G1 and a 16 GB heap; young pauses are 40-80 ms and full-heap marking takes several seconds. The team proposes moving to a 32 GB node and a 24 GB heap "because the map takes about 800 MB (50M x 16 bytes)". Observed live set after refresh is about 4.5 GB.
questions.promptHtml: Why is the live set so much larger than 800 MB, and what would you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add memory." It doesn't estimate per-entry cost and misses that the real problem is boxed nodes and pointer-rich layout.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are keys dense or sparse? Are values only a bitmask (fits a long)? Read/write ratio? Is lookup latency or footprint the priority? Is the map replaced wholesale daily (so immutability is possible)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed urgently; this is capacity and pause-time work. Keep the heap at the current size while redesigning.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Boxing and HashMap node overhead explain it; the table array and GC marking cost are secondary.
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap histogram jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram (expect HashMap$Node, java.lang.Long), JOL for sizes, a heap dump in MAT to confirm dominators.
  5. Root cause (the math, compressed oops): per entry = HashMap.Node (12 header + 4 hash + 3 refs x 4 = 28, padded to 32) + key Long (12 + 8, aligned to 24) + value Long 24 = 80 bytes. 50M x 80 = 4.0 GB, plus the table: 50M / 0.75 = 66.7M needs capacity 2^27, but 2^26 x 0.75 = 50.3M, so capacity 2^26 = 67.1M slots x 4 B = 268 MB. Total about 4.3 GB, matching 4.5 GB observed. The "16 bytes" estimate counted only the payload; overhead is 5x.
  6. Fix: Replace with primitive structures: two parallel long[] sorted by key and binary search (50M x 16 = 800 MB, 2 ops of cache-friendly search), or an open-addressing long-to-long map (FastUtil Long2LongOpenHashMap, Eclipse Collections, etc.) at load factor ~0.5-0.75 costing about 1.1-1.6 GB. Arrays of primitives have no per-object headers and only a few objects to mark, so GC marking becomes trivial. Because the data is rebuilt daily, build the new structure off to the side and swap one reference (immutable, safely published; a volatile field).
final class SegmentIndex {                // immutable snapshot
    final long[] keys, vals;              // keys sorted ascending
    long get(long k) { int i = Arrays.binarySearch(keys, k); return i >= 0 ? vals[i] : 0L; }
}
static volatile SegmentIndex current;     // swap on refresh
  1. Prevention: Capacity model in design reviews (bytes per entry), a heap-histogram check in load tests, a rule to avoid boxed maps above ~10M entries.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not move to a 24 GB heap: more memory does not fix pointer chasing, and bigger heaps lengthen marking. Sorted arrays make O(log n) lookups (~26 probes; fine versus a network call); updates need a rebuild. If lookups are hot, use open addressing. Stay under the compressed-oops limit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Keys are sparse 128-bit UUIDs? → Two longs per key in an open-addressing table or a byte[]-slab hash; same technique.
  • Memory-map the file instead? → Off-heap, lazily paged by the OS, near-zero GC cost; use a read-only MappedByteBuffer (watch page-fault latency on cold start).
  • Does Long cache help? → Only -128..127; irrelevant here.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team doubled node size twice to host a boxed map; the third attempt used primitive arrays and shrank the service to a third of its fleet.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "16 bytes per entry", suggests more RAM.
  • Hire: explains boxing/node overhead and proposes primitive collections.
  • Strong hire: does the per-entry math, quantifies GC mark effect, designs immutable snapshot swap and weighs mmap and open addressing.

questions.promptHtml: What is Class Data Sharing (CDS/AppCDS), and how does it relate to the newer AOT cache? When would you use them for a containerised service?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Startup and footprint tuning without changing the language; checks awareness of JDK-provided features before jumping to native image.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CDS stores pre-parsed, pre-verified class metadata in a memory-mapped archive so the JVM skips parsing and verification at startup and can share the pages between processes. Since JDK 12 a default archive for JDK classes ships and is on by default; AppCDS adds your application classes. JDK 24's AOT cache (JEP 483) goes further by caching classes in loaded and linked state. They cut startup, not peak performance.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Timeline (verify against each version): JDK 5 CDS for JDK classes; JDK 10 AppCDS; JDK 12 default CDS archive; JDK 13 dynamic archiving -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit; JDK 19 -XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive -XX:SharedArchiveFile=...; JDK 24 AOT class loading and linking (JEP 483) with -XX:AOTMode=record/create, -XX:AOTCache.
  • Flow for JDK 24+: record a training run, create the cache, then run with -XX:AOTCache=app.aot. Constraints from the JEP: same JDK release, architecture and OS; matching classpath (extra entries appended allowed); JARs only; only classes from the built-in loaders are cached, not user-defined loaders. If unusable, it warns and continues.
  • Benefits: faster startup (class parse/verify skipped), lower per-process memory because archive pages are shared across JVMs on the same node (read-only mapped).
  • Later releases extend the cache with profile data; I believe JEP 515 adds method profiles in a later release; verify before relying on it.
  • Spring Boot documents CDS support for building the archive in the image (verify version-specific steps and flags in the Spring docs).
  • Operationally: generate the archive in the CI image build, not at pod start, from the exact JDK and jar that ship; treat a mismatched archive as a silent-fallback risk and check logs (-Xshare:auto falls back; -Xshare:on fails fast).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# JDK 19+ dynamic archive, created automatically on first run and reused:
java -XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive -XX:SharedArchiveFile=/opt/app/app.jsa -jar app.jar
# JDK 24+ AOT cache:
java -XX:AOTMode=record -XX:AOTConfiguration=app.aotconf -cp app.jar com.example.App
java -XX:AOTMode=create -XX:AOTConfiguration=app.aotconf -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp app.jar
java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp app.jar com.example.App

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Building the archive on a developer laptop JDK and shipping it to a different JDK build.
  • Expecting CDS to improve throughput or JIT warmup (it doesn't remove JIT work).
  • Forgetting archives need writable paths in read-only containers when auto-creating.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What's the difference from native image? → CDS keeps the normal JVM and JIT; native image is a closed-world AOT binary. See the native image scenario.
  2. Does it save memory? → Yes, shared mapped pages across processes and less metadata parsed per JVM.
  3. How do you confirm it's used? → -Xshare:on fails if unusable; -Xlog:cds and class+load logs show "shared objects file".

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE has not heard of it or says "faster startup". Senior knows the lineage, the build-time workflow in CI, the matching constraints and what it does not fix (JIT warmup).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Baking an AppCDS archive into the image cut cold-start class loading from several seconds to well under that, shortening scale-out lag without changing code.

questions.promptHtml: What is deoptimization in HotSpot? Give examples of what triggers it, and how would you detect it hurting a production service?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows understanding that JIT code is speculative; deopt storms explain "fast, then suddenly slow" incidents.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: C2 compiles using assumptions from profiles, for example "this branch is never taken" or "this call site only sees one class". When an assumption fails, the code hits an uncommon trap, execution falls back to the interpreter at that point, the compiled method is marked "not entrant", and the method gets recompiled later. A few are normal; repeated cycles mean a deopt storm with latency spikes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Mechanism: compiled code contains uncommon traps (not generated for never-seen paths, keeping code small and fast). Hitting one reconstructs interpreter frames from the compiled frame state (debug info), continues in the interpreter, and records the reason so recompilation can avoid repeating the speculation.
  • Common reasons: unstable_if (a branch that was never taken now is), class_check / bimorphic (new receiver type at an inlined virtual call), null_check, range_check, unloaded class (class not yet loaded when compiled), class hierarchy changes invalidating CHA-based devirtualisation (loading a new subclass).
  • Timeline: compiled -> trap -> "made not entrant" -> interpreter/C1 -> recompiled at C2 with updated profile. With thousands of methods affected by one new class load (e.g. first request of a rare type), the stall is visible as a CPU burst and latency blip.
  • Detection: -XX:+PrintCompilation lines containing "made not entrant"; unified logging for deoptimization (I believe -Xlog:deoptimization=debug in recent JDKs; verify); JFR events jdk.Deoptimization; rising compile-queue length and jdk.Compilation.
  • Mitigation: warm with representative traffic (the right type mix), avoid polymorphism at hot call sites, avoid surprise class loading under load (preload), and don't blame flags first. If a single method repeatedly deopts, it can hit PerMethodRecompilationCutoff and be left at a lower tier (verify default).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface Codec { int enc(int x); }
final class A implements Codec { public int enc(int x){ return x+1; } }
final class B implements Codec { public int enc(int x){ return x*2; } }
// Warm with only A: C2 inlines A.enc and guards with a class check.
// First call with B => class_check trap => deopt, then bimorphic/megamorphic recompile.
static int hot(Codec c, int n){ int s=0; for(int i=0;i<n;i++) s+=c.enc(i); return s; }
java -XX:+PrintCompilation -jar app.jar | grep "made not entrant"
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=deopt.jfr settings=profile   # inspect jdk.Deoptimization

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating every "made not entrant" line as a bug; many are routine tier transitions.
  • Warming with a synthetic workload that pollutes or under-represents types.
  • Assuming a restart "fixes" it; it just resets the profile.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is CHA? → Class Hierarchy Analysis: the compiler treats a method as monomorphic if no loaded subclass overrides it; loading one later invalidates that code.
  2. How does it relate to megamorphic calls? → Past 2 receiver types inline caches degrade to vtable/itable dispatch; see Shipilev's megamorphic quark.
  3. Can a deopt storm be caused by a deploy? → Yes: new traffic mixes or lazily loaded subclasses change profiles; correlate JFR deopt counts with request patterns.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "JIT may recompile". Senior can name uncommon traps, CHA invalidation, and show how to spot a storm with JFR or logs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feature flag enabled a rarely-seen subclass at 10:00; p99 spiked for 20 s as hundreds of CHA-dependent methods deoptimised and recompiled.

questions.promptHtml: Why is object allocation on the JVM so cheap, and what is a TLAB? When does allocation leave the fast path?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand allocation as bump-pointer in thread-local buffers and can connect that to allocation-rate GC pressure and contention.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each thread gets a Thread-Local Allocation Buffer, a private chunk of eden. Allocating an object is "bump the pointer, check against the end": a handful of instructions with no locking. When the TLAB is full the thread gets a new one (a synchronised, slower step); very large objects bypass the TLAB and allocate directly in the heap, which is slower and for G1 may mean humongous allocation. The cost that remains is not the allocation but the GC work that high allocation rate causes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
eden: [ TLAB(t1) ][ TLAB(t2) ][ TLAB(t3) ] ... free ...
TLAB(t1): [obj][obj][obj] ^top ........ ^end   alloc = top += size; if top > end -> slow path
  • Fast path (JIT-inlined): load top, add size, compare with end, store. Memory is pre-zeroed per the Java guarantee, which costs bandwidth but not locking.
  • Slow paths: (1) TLAB refill when the remaining space is too small (the JVM may retain the TLAB and allocate this object outside it if the remainder is large, governed by an adaptive waste limit); (2) object bigger than the TLAB goes through shared-heap allocation with atomic/lock; (3) eden exhausted triggers a young GC.
  • TLAB sizes adapt per thread from allocation history; -XX:+UseTLAB is on by default. Tuning flags exist (TLABSize, TLABWasteTargetPercent; verify defaults), but they are rarely the right fix.
  • Evidence: JFR events jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB and jdk.ObjectAllocationOutsideTLAB show what allocates; in JFR allocation profiling, "outside TLAB" samples highlight large or refill-heavy sites. Related quarks by Shipilev: TLAB Allocation, TLABs and Heap Parsability.
  • Implication: millions of short-lived small objects are cheap to create and cheap to collect if they die young, but they still burn memory bandwidth and trigger more frequent young GCs. Escape analysis can remove some.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
byte[] big = new byte[8 * 1024 * 1024];   // likely outside a TLAB; with G1 and region size 4 MB this is humongous
for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) { var p = new int[]{i, i + 1}; sink(p); }  // TLAB fast path each time
jcmd <pid> JFR.start settings=profile duration=60s filename=alloc.jfr
jfr print --events jdk.ObjectAllocationOutsideTLAB alloc.jfr | head

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "allocation is expensive in Java" or "is always O(1) and free"; it's cheap per object but total rate matters.
  • Pooling small objects to "save allocation": usually slower than TLAB allocation plus young GC, and it makes more objects survive to old gen.
  • Ignoring large-array allocation sites in hot paths.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does allocation rate drive? → Young GC frequency (rate / eden size); detail in the GC chunks.
  2. Why is a TLAB per thread a problem for thousands of threads? → Many partly used TLABs waste eden; adaptive sizing shrinks them.
  3. How do you find top allocators? → JFR allocation events or async-profiler -e alloc, which report by stack trace.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "new is cheap". Senior describes the bump-pointer fast path, the three slow paths and how to profile allocation by stack.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 4 MB buffer allocated per request caused 3 GB/s allocation outside TLABs and constant young GCs until buffers were pooled (the exception where pooling is right: large, fixed-size buffers).

questions.promptHtml: What is the JVM code cache? What happens when it fills up, and how do you monitor and size it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A rare, nasty failure mode: the JVM keeps running but silently becomes slow.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The code cache is the native memory region where the JVM stores generated machine code: interpreter stubs and JIT-compiled methods. With tiered compilation its reserved size is 240 MB by default. If it fills, the JVM logs "CodeCache is full. Compiler has been disabled", stops JIT compiling, and the service degrades to running whatever is already compiled plus the interpreter, with no exception.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Source: the java launcher docs list ReservedCodeCacheSize default 240 MB with tiered compilation and 48 MB without.
  • Since Java 9 it is segmented: non-method code, profiled code (C1 tier 2/3, short-lived), non-profiled code (C1 tier 1 and C2, long-lived). Segmentation reduces fragmentation and makes sweeping cheaper; the sizes are derived from the total unless set (-XX:NonNMethodCodeHeapSize, ProfiledCodeHeapSize, NonProfiledCodeHeapSize).
  • Code is evicted when methods are deoptimised or become cold (-XX:+UseCodeCacheFlushing, default on in modern JDKs; verify). A leak of generated classes (Groovy scripts, proxies per request) also produces compiled code that can't be reclaimed until the class unloads.
  • Symptoms: sudden throughput drop after hours, CPU shift from application threads to the interpreter, "CodeCache is full" in stdout, JIT compile count flat. Often hits services with huge codebases, many generated classes, or aggressive inlining.
  • Monitoring: jcmd <pid> Compiler.codecache, MXBeans (CodeHeap 'non-profiled nmethods', etc.), Micrometer jvm_memory_used_bytes{id=~"CodeHeap.*"}, -XX:+PrintCodeCache (verify naming per JDK).
  • Fix order: find why it is filling (class generation leak) before raising -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=512m; reserved, not committed, so a larger value costs address space and only commits as used.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
jcmd <pid> Compiler.codecache
# size in use vs max_used vs free for each segment
java -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=512m -XX:+UseCodeCacheFlushing -jar app.jar

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Seeing no Java exception and concluding the service is healthy while latency creeps.
  • Raising the size without examining class generation.
  • Forgetting code cache counts in RSS when it fills.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is -XX:+PrintCompilation going to show when it is full? → New compilations stop appearing and the warning appears.
  2. Do native image binaries have one? → No code cache or JIT; the code is in the executable.
  3. Why is the profiled segment short-lived? → Tier 3 code carries profiling overhead and is replaced by C2 code.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE has never heard of it. Senior states the default, the silent-degradation behaviour, the segmented layout and how to monitor it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A large monolith with heavy reflection and generated proxies slowly degraded over a day; the only evidence was a one-line "CodeCache is full" in stdout, caught by adding a log alert.

questions.contextHtml:
A pricing service (Java 17, G1, 4 GiB heap, 6 GiB pod) evaluates tenant-defined discount rules written in Groovy. Every 3 weeks it OOMs; this time it started restarting daily after a marketing campaign raised traffic from 50 to 400 RPS. jstat -gc shows heap OK (old gen 35%) but MU (Metaspace used) climbs about 120 MB/hour; jvm_classes_loaded_classes rises from 40k to 600k over 8 hours. Log at death: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace. Code:

public double price(Order o, String ruleSource) {
    GroovyShell shell = new GroovyShell();              // new GroovyClassLoader inside
    Script s = shell.parse(ruleSource);                 // compiles source into a new class every call
    Binding b = new Binding(); b.setVariable("order", o);
    s.setBinding(b);
    return ((Number) s.run()).doubleValue();
}

Nobody sets -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, how do you prove it, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase Metaspace" or "there is a memory leak in Groovy". It does not recognise that the app generates a class per call and doesn't know when classes unload.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many distinct rule sources versus calls? Do rule sources change often? Is the Groovy rule trusted (security)? Are there other generators (proxies, templates)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Set -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m so failure is crisp and bounded; add an alert on classes loaded; restart on a schedule while fixing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Class-per-call from parse with a new loader each time; (b) loaders pinned by something (a cache or static listing scripts) so they cannot unload; (c) other generators; (d) JIT/code cache growth consequently.
  4. How I'd verify each: jcmd <pid> VM.classloader_stats (thousands of GroovyClassLoader$InnerLoader instances), jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram | grep -i script, -Xlog:class+load rate against traffic, -Xlog:class+unload showing few unloads, a heap dump in MAT for who retains the loaders (GC roots path).
  5. Root cause: Each call compiles the rule text into a fresh class Script123456 in a new loader. At 400 RPS that is 1.4M classes per hour. A class unloads only when its loader is unreachable and a GC runs; here Groovy's internal caches and metaclass registry (MetaClassRegistry) hold references, so many are never unloaded, and even those that could unload do so only at GC time, which lags allocation. Metaspace is native and uncapped, so it grows until the pod nears 6 GiB.
  6. Fix: Short-term: cache compiled scripts keyed by a hash of the source and reuse the compiled Script class, creating a new instance per run (instances are cheap, scripts are not thread-safe so don't share instances).
private final ConcurrentMap<String, Class<? extends Script>> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
private final GroovyShell shell = new GroovyShell();

public double price(Order o, String src) throws Exception {
    Class<? extends Script> c = cache.computeIfAbsent(sha256(src), k -> shell.getClassLoader().parseClass(src));
    Script s = InvokerHelper.createScript(c, new Binding(Map.of("order", o)));
    return ((Number) s.run()).doubleValue();
}

Long-term: bound the cache (Caffeine with max size, eviction), compile rules at tenant-config-save time, consider replacing a general scripting engine with a restricted expression language (CEL, SpEL, rules as data) for security and cost. 7. Prevention: Metaspace cap and alert on jvm_classes_loaded_classes slope; code review rule "no compile-per-request"; load test with realistic rule diversity. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just increase MaxMetaspaceSize (delays the crash), not force System.gc() periodically, and not share Script instances across threads. A cache keyed by unbounded tenant-supplied text needs a size bound, or it becomes the new leak.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cache hits are 100% but classes still climb? → Another generator: check class names in the histogram ($Proxy, CGLIB, lambdas) and loader stats.
  • Why didn't G1 unload them? → Loaders still reachable via caches or thread contexts; unloading only for unreachable loaders.
  • Rules change hourly per tenant; does the cache keep old versions? → Evict by tenant+version key with size/time bounds so old classes can unload.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a rules feature shipped to "handful of tenants", grew 100x, and the first symptom was RSS creeping while heap graphs stayed flat; MaxMetaspaceSize at least converted it to a loud failure.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raises limits or blames Groovy.
  • Hire: spots compile-per-call, caches compiled classes, sets a Metaspace cap.
  • Strong hire: explains unloading rules, proves with classloader stats and unload logs, bounds the cache, and questions the scripting design.

questions.contextHtml: A platform team cuts cost by moving 120 Java 17 microservice pods from 4 CPU / 8 GiB to limits: cpu 1500m, memory 1536Mi (requests equal), JVM flags unchanged: just -XX:+UseContainerSupport defaults, no -Xmx. After rollout, services show p99 from 80 ms to 600 ms, with 300-400 ms stalls every few seconds. container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total is climbing. GC log first line: Using Serial. Heap is auto-sized to about 384 MiB and the old gen fills quickly. JVM startup log: Runtime.availableProcessors() = 2. A team lead suggests adding -XX:+UseG1GC and moving on.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the behaviour and propose a better configuration.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Force G1" or "give them more CPU". It misses ergonomics (what the JVM decided and why), CFS throttling and the memory split.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What are the services' live set sizes and allocation rates? Latency SLO? Are these CPU-bound or I/O-bound? What are Kubernetes CPU request vs limit semantics here (limit enforced via CFS quota)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the worst services to the previous size, or raise CPU limit to 2 and memory to 2 GiB for the latency-critical ones; set explicit -XX:MaxRAMPercentage.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Ergonomics picked Serial GC because the container looks like a non-server-class machine (fewer than 2 CPUs or less than ~1792 MB selects Serial; with 1536 MiB memory the JVM treats it as non-server; verify for your JDK); (b) heap defaulted to 25% of 1536 MiB = 384 MiB, too small for the live set, causing frequent full-ish collections; (c) CFS throttling: more runnable threads (GC, JIT, app) than quota allows, so the container is paused for the rest of each 100 ms period; (d) availableProcessors() = 2 from a 1.5 CPU quota (rounded up) sizes pools and parallel GC for 2 CPUs while only 1.5 are really available.
  4. How I'd verify each: -Xlog:gc* and -Xlog:gc+init (collector, heap, workers), jcmd <pid> VM.flags, java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -XX:+PrintContainerInfo (verify flag name for your JDK; -Xlog:os+container also works), cgroup cpu.stat (nr_throttled, throttled_usec), JFR jdk.CPULoad/GC events, jstat -gcutil.
  5. Root cause: Math: 1536 MiB x 25% = 384 MiB heap; with Serial a young+old collection is single-threaded and stop-the-world; a 250 MB old-gen full collection takes ~300 ms on one throttled core. Meanwhile throttling means any burst above 150 ms CPU per 100 ms period stalls everything. GC and JIT threads steal quota from request threads.
  6. Fix: Choose per service, not blanket. For 1.5 CPU / 1.5 GiB: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=65 -XX:+UseSerialGC is acceptable for small heaps if pauses fit the SLO; for latency-critical ones, at least 2 CPUs and 2 GiB and an explicit -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=2. Cut JIT/GC thread counts where needed (-XX:CICompilerCount, -XX:ParallelGCThreads), and drop CPU limits in favour of requests only if platform policy allows (throttling disappears, but noisy-neighbour risk rises).
JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=65 -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=2 -Xlog:gc*:stdout:time"
  1. Prevention: A rightsizing checklist (live set x 2-3, allocation rate, p99 SLO), per-service load test at target limits, dashboards for throttling and GC pause, startup log of effective flags.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use the same flags for 120 services; not set heap near 90% to "use the RAM"; not keep an old copy of JDK flags that disable container support. Note that on cgroup v2 and newer JDKs (cgroup v2 support arrived in 15, with backports; verify) container detection works; older JDKs may ignore limits.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• CPU limit 1000m exactly: availableProcessors? → 1, which also selects Serial and single-threaded pools by default.
  • Why not remove limits? → Throttling disappears, but the scheduler cannot protect neighbours; use requests plus node-level policy.
  • Would a CPU quota of 1.5 benefit from more threads? → No; more runnable threads than quota only increases throttling.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a cost program saved 40% on paper but p99 doubled on tier-1 services, and the dashboards showing throttled periods were never looked at until the SLO page fired.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: flips collector or blames the platform.
  • Hire: understands Serial selection, 25% default heap, and throttling, and gives per-service flags.
  • Strong hire: quotes the ergonomics rules with verification, uses cgroup stats, and proposes a measured rightsizing process.

questions.contextHtml: A company runs two Spring Boot 3 / Java 21 services: (A) a nightly-triggered report generator on AWS Lambda-style infrastructure with a 700 ms cold-start budget, currently 6.5 s; (B) a 24/7 pricing API at 3,000 RPS per instance with p99 = 25 ms, 4 vCPU, 4 GiB RSS. Management read that native image gives "10x faster startup and lower memory" and asks to convert both. Build time budget on CI is 10 minutes; reflection-heavy libraries (Jackson with dynamic types, Hibernate, a plugin SPI loaded by classpath scanning) are used in both.
questions.promptHtml: Would you convert A, B, both or neither, and how do you decide?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes to both, native is faster", or "No, it is immature". Both ignore the closed-world trade-offs and the actual constraints per service.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is startup or peak throughput the business metric? What is the instance lifetime and how often does it scale? What libraries rely on reflection, dynamic proxies, classpath scanning? Who is on call for native-specific failures? Is Oracle GraalVM licensing acceptable versus the Community Edition (a point to verify)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident. First take cheap wins on A: AppCDS / AOT cache (JEP 483, Java 24+) and lazy init, then measure.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Native suits A (short-lived, cold-start dominated); B is dominated by peak throughput and tail latency where JIT with profile data tends to win, so native may regress.
  4. How I'd verify each: Build a native binary of each with the Spring AOT/Native Build Tools plugin and benchmark: startup time to first response, RSS at idle and under load, throughput and p99 with k6/wrk at steady state, build time and CI cost; run the full test suite in native mode (nativeTest), not only JVM mode.
  5. Root cause / mechanism: Native image compiles ahead-of-time under a closed-world assumption: everything reachable must be known at build time. That removes class loading, interpretation and warmup, hence ms-scale start and smaller RSS. It also removes the JIT, so no profile-guided speculation (peak throughput commonly lower unless using PGO, available in Oracle GraalVM; verify), and reflection, proxies, resources and JNI need hints (reachability metadata) generated by the build tooling or maintained by hand. GC options are limited (Serial by default; G1 for native image is an Oracle GraalVM feature; verify per version).
  6. Fix / decision: Convert A (cold start 6.5 s -> well under budget is typical in vendor claims; I'd measure, not assume). Keep B on the JVM, using CDS/AOT cache and warmup for its startup issue; revisit if instance churn grows. For A, mitigate native pitfalls: generate metadata via the tracing agent in tests, fail CI on missing reflection hints, and keep a JVM fallback build.
./mvnw -Pnative native:compile            # Spring Boot native build; needs GraalVM JDK
./target/report-gen                      # compare against java -jar baseline
  1. Prevention: Run integration tests against the native artifact in CI, pin library versions that ship reachability metadata, document debugging limits (no JFR parity in all builds, different tooling; verify), and track build duration.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not convert B for cost reasons without measured throughput; a native binary needing 30% more instances negates savings. I would not migrate without removing runtime classpath scanning and dynamic proxies in a test environment first. Observability, heap dumps and profiling work differently, so ensure the on-call tooling exists.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• B needs faster autoscale only. → CDS/AOT cache plus warmup and slow-start; or CRaC where supported (verify).
  • Native build takes 18 minutes on CI. → Build only on release branches, use remote build caches, run the JVM-mode tests per PR.
  • Dynamic plugin loading by users? → Incompatible with closed world; keep the JVM.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team shipped a native image and found a rarely used endpoint failed at runtime with a missing reflection entry; only the JVM-mode tests had run.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: yes/no without reasoning.
  • Hire: segments by workload and cites closed-world/JIT trade-offs.
  • Strong hire: proposes measurement plan, CI native testing, intermediate options (CDS/AOT cache, CRaC), and operational readiness.

questions.contextHtml: Platform FinOps wants to halve memory for 200 pods of a Java 21 gateway service from 8 GiB to 4 GiB. Today: -Xmx5g, G1, 8 GiB limit. Steady-state: heap used after GC about 1.1 GB, peak committed heap 3.2 GB; container_memory_working_set_bytes about 6.0 GiB; request rate 1,200 RPS; 350 platform threads; Netty direct buffers hover at 600 MB; Metaspace 180 MB; code cache 70 MB. Product wants no p99 regression (today 45 ms) and no new restarts.
questions.promptHtml: How would you decide the new memory configuration, and what do you do before changing 200 pods?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set -Xmx2g and limit 4Gi". It guesses the budget and ignores unaccounted RSS, GC headroom and burst behaviour.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the worst-case traffic burst versus average? What is the allocation rate (drives eden size)? Why is RSS 6.0 GiB if heap is 3.2 GB peak committed (where do 2.8 GB go)? Are direct buffers bounded? Acceptable failure budget?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; this is planned work with a canary.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Heap is over-provisioned: live 1.1 GB, so 2-2.5 GB heap likely suffices if pause/allocation targets hold; (b) non-heap is bigger than assumed: direct 600 + Metaspace 180 + code 70 + threads 350 x 1 MB = 350 + GC structures ~300 + malloc/other ~300 = about 1.8 GB; (c) G1 releases heap lazily, so RSS includes heap that is committed but idle; (d) peak bursts may push direct buffers or heap higher.
  4. How I'd verify each: One canary with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, compare jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary against RSS; GC logs -Xlog:gc* for post-GC occupancy, pause times and humongous allocations; Micrometer for direct buffers and threads; run a load test at 2x peak with the target config; watch p99, GC pause, container_memory_working_set_bytes.
  5. Root cause of waste: -Xmx5g with a 1.1 GB live set let the heap grow with no pressure. Budget math for new config: heap 2.0 GB (live 1.1 GB x ~1.8 headroom for young gen and spikes) + non-heap about 1.8 GB = 3.8 GB, leaving only about 200 MB of headroom in 4 GiB, too thin. Before shrinking the limit, cut non-heap: cap direct memory at 400 MB with pooled-buffer tuning, set -Xss512k for known-shallow stacks (350 x 0.5 MB saves ~175 MB), reduce arenas with MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 (verify effect by measuring). Then target heap 1.8-2 GB + non-heap about 1.5 GB = 3.5 GB in a 4.5 GiB limit.
  6. Fix: Roll out in stages: canary 1 pod, then 5%, 25%, 100%; each stage with automatic rollback on p99 or restart regression. Use percentage flags to keep config proportional (-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=50) or explicit -Xmx when the budget is stable.
env:
  - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
    value: "-Xmx2g -Xss512k -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=400m -XX:+UseG1GC -Xlog:gc*:stdout:time"
resources: { requests: { memory: 4608Mi }, limits: { memory: 4608Mi } }
  1. Prevention: A per-service memory budget doc (heap, metaspace, threads, direct, other), alerts at 85% of the limit, and a pre-merge check of effective JVM flags.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not choose the limit from average usage; peaks and GC headroom matter more. A smaller heap raises GC frequency (check CPU cost), and less headroom raises OOM-kill risk. I'd accept 4.5 GiB (a 44% cut) with a safety margin rather than the full 4 GiB target, and say so to FinOps with the data.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• G1 returns memory slowly; can RSS be reduced further? → Periodic uncommit options differ by collector and version (verify, e.g. G1 periodic uncommit behaviour and ZGC uncommit); measure before relying on them.
  • What if traffic doubles next quarter? → The budget scales with allocation rate and threads more than with RPS directly; re-run the load test and revisit.
  • Why not many smaller pods? → Fixed per-JVM overhead (Metaspace, code cache, runtime) multiplies; fewer larger pods share it, but bigger pods raise blast radius.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a memory-diet project cut limits by guessing from heap graphs, then three weeks later a traffic burst grew direct buffers and the kernel killed a third of the fleet within minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: guesses numbers from heap alone.
  • Hire: budgets heap plus non-heap, tests under load, rolls out with canary.
  • Strong hire: uses NMT to reconcile RSS, trims non-heap (threads, direct, arenas), keeps explicit headroom, and quantifies GC/CPU trade-offs.
